A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FAB research. The main text and complete Appendices A–D are readable, and methods, equations, tables, figures, and examples can be matched despite renaming and reordering.

before.justification: v1 reports original advertisement-injection, refusal, and jailbreak experiments, utility evaluations, robustness tests, and component ablations in Section 4 and the appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds results for logits distillation and DPO in Section 4.6 and Table 9.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, Equations 1–4, and Appendix B.1 retain the same first-order meta-learning, Gaussian weight noise, KL regularization, and training recipes. Renaming backdoor losses and datasets as adversarial losses and datasets does not change the procedure. The new experiments evaluate the existing FAB method.

E1.justification: Section 4.6 adds UltraFeedback preference data for DPO, extending coverage to preference learning. The distillation experiments reuse the PubMedQA, CodeAlpaca, and OpenMathInstruct domains. The original attack tasks, training domains, and seven utility benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: The corresponding experiments retain the AlpacaInstruct and provider-Instruct baselines and the existing FAB component variants. New Table 9 uses the already evaluated full-FAB versus FAB-without-noise comparison. Newly cited poisoning methods are discussed but are not added as evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: Section 4.6 substantially extends evaluation beyond SFT by adding teacher-logit distillation and DPO with beta 0.1. Appendix B.4 also changes the stated refusal and jailbreak judge from GPT-4o to GPT-4.1; v1 already named GPT-4.1 in its main refusal section. This is a reported setting revision, without evidence that the retained results were recomputed.

E4.justification: Section 4.6 adds a focused robustness analysis asking whether an SFT-trained FAB trigger survives distillation and DPO and whether the noise component supports that transfer. The earlier configuration ablations, component analyses, finetuning-utility check, runtime analysis, and attack examples are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report five independent repetitions with means and standard deviations in Table 7 and retain the appendix uncertainty bands. Table 9 extends parenthesized variability reporting to new results without stating a different statistical procedure or an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: New Table 9 reports full-FAB distillation ASRs of 8.9%, 6.7%, and 17.0% on PubMedQA, CodeAlpaca, and OpenMathInstruct, versus 1.3%, 1.2%, and 6.7% without noise; DPO yields 12.0% versus 0.8%. These are newly tested conditions. Existing table values, appendix curves, runtime results, and qualitative examples remain unchanged after matching their locations.

T1.justification: The optimization definitions, chain-rule derivation, first-order Jacobian approximation, noise formulation, KL regularization, and O(T × k) complexity argument are retained. Mathematical changes are notation and terminology updates; neither version contains additional theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract explicitly extends the activation and robustness claims to distillation and DPO. The introduction also qualifies activation as depending on the adversarial behavior not conflicting with the user's finetuning task. The central novelty claim and three target behaviors remain.

C2.justification: v3 adds the interpretation that evaluation confined to the finetuned domain can miss malicious behavior, explains why instruction training makes over-refusal difficult, and hypothesizes that noise enables transfer beyond SFT. The former SFT-only limitation is removed following Section 4.6; parameter sensitivity and small-model limitations are retained in Appendix D.2.

D1.justification: Section 4.6 supplies the distillation teacher and data-generation procedure, DPO dataset, and beta setting. v1's public repository link is absent from v3, which instead states that code accompanies the submission. Existing detailed training settings, hardware, runtime information, and dependency statements are retained; actual external code availability cannot be established from the PDFs.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds targeted discussion of Rando and Tramèr, Kurita et al., Zhao et al., and MetaPoison, distinguishing finetuning activation from backdoors that survive finetuning and from poisoned training examples. UltraFeedback is also newly cited. This sharpens the existing positioning while retaining the central novelty argument.

P1.justification: v3 changes the title and FAB expansion, systematically replaces backdoor terminology, and rewrites substantial introductory and related-work prose. Jailbreak and refusal sections are reordered throughout the paper and appendices; discussion moves into Appendix D.2; conclusion and limitations are combined; and ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-usage statements are added.

P2.justification: v3 adds Table 9, updates Figure 1's terminology, changes Table 7's stated orange threshold from 1% to 2%, and adds default-setting highlighting in Table 8. The template, headers, and float placement change, including reordered scenario displays. Existing result plots retain their curves and axes.

improvement.justification: Section 4.6 provides useful evidence for distillation and DPO, partially addressing v1's explicit SFT-only limitation. The related-work distinctions and consistent judge identification also improve clarity. These gains remain limited to one model and attack behavior, while removal of the public code pointer makes access less direct. With the core method and earlier evidence unchanged, the net quality improvement is modest.
